title: Comparison of adjectives; adverbs

objectives.can: Recognise comparative and superlative forms, the two ways of saying 'than', and the formation of adverbs.

explanation.summary: Latin adjectives have three degrees: the plain (positive) degree, the comparative ('stronger') and the superlative ('strongest'). The comparative and superlative are made by endings, not by separate words as in 'more' and 'most'. Adverbs are formed from adjectives by other endings. The Vulgate uses all of these constantly, and each has its own way of saying 'than'.

sections.heading: Three degrees
body: The positive degree is the adjective as you already know it: *fortis*, 'strong'. The comparative adds -ior (masculine and feminine) or -ius (neuter) to the stem: *fortior*, 'stronger' or 'rather strong'. The superlative adds -issimus, -issima, -issimum: *fortissimus*, 'strongest' or 'very strong'. The stem is found by dropping the genitive ending of the positive: alt- from *altus*, fort- from *fortis*.

A comparative is declined like a third-declension adjective with consonant stem: the masculine and feminine share one form (*fortior*), the neuter has -ius (*fortius*), and the other cases are built on the stem fortior- (the accusative singular *fortiorem*). The superlative is declined like *bonus*, a first and second declension adjective, so its endings are the ones you know (*altissimus*, *altissima*, *altissimum*). The comparative is not a third-declension i-stem, so its ablative singular is usually -e and its genitive plural -um (*fortiorum*).

Translation needs care. A comparative with no 'than' often means 'rather' or 'too'; a superlative often means no more than 'very': *carissimus* is 'dearest', but is also the ordinary word for 'dear friend', as at the head of a letter.

sections.heading: Adjectives that do not follow the pattern
body: A few of the commonest adjectives take their degrees from a different stem. *bonus* gives *melior* and *optimus*; *malus* gives *pejor* (the edition's spelling) and *pessimus*; *magnus* gives *majora* (neuter plural) and *maximus*; *parvus* gives *minor* and *minimus*; and *multus* gives *plus* and *plurimus*. Learn each pair with its positive: the texts file the comparative and superlative under the positive's headword, so *melior* and *optimus* are forms of *bonus*.

Some adjectives with stems in -r have the superlative -errimus instead of -issimus: *pulcher* gives *pulcherrimus*, *acer* gives *acerrimus*, *celeber* gives *celeberrimus*. A few others in -lis (*facilis*, *similis*) have -illimus. Forms that are both rare and unusual are not drawn in the exercises, but those that occur in the texts are in the readings.

sections.heading: Two ways of saying 'than'
body: After a comparative, 'than' is expressed in one of two ways. The first is *quam* followed by a second item in the same case as the first. In *Melius est nubere quam uri* the two infinitives are compared. The verse is 1 Corinthians 7:9. The second is the ablative of comparison: the thing compared stands alone in the ablative and no word for 'than' is used. *Fortior me*, 'stronger than I', has *me* in the ablative.

The ablative of comparison is neat and short, but it is used only where the second term would otherwise be a nominative or accusative; when it would stand in another case, or is an infinitive or a clause, *quam* is used. Both constructions are common in the Vulgate, and a verse may even use one beside the other. When you see a comparative, look at once for its 'than': either *quam* or a word in the ablative.

sections.heading: Adverbs from adjectives
body: Latin makes most of its adverbs from adjectives. An adjective of the first and second declension takes -e (*pulcher*, *pulchre*). An adjective of the third declension takes -iter or -ter (*fortis*, *fortiter*; *prudens*, *prudenter*; *diligens*, *diligenter*; *velox*, *velociter*). The adverb is invariable: it has no case, number or gender, and it modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

Many of the commonest adverbs are not made in this way and have to be learned: *valde*, *nimis*, *semper*, *statim*, *simul*. The comparative adverb is the neuter singular of the comparative adjective (*longius*, 'further'), and the superlative adverb ends in -e, built on the superlative adjective. For this reason a comparative in -ius may be an adverb or a neuter adjective; the sentence decides.

misunderstandings: A superlative does not always mean 'the most'. Very often it simply means 'very': *Altissimus* is used of God as 'the Most High', and *carissimus* is just 'dear'. Where no group is mentioned for the comparison, 'very' is usually the better sense.
A comparative is not always followed by 'than'. Without a second term it means 'rather', 'too' or just 'more', and the context must supply the sense.

A comparative in -ius is not necessarily an adverb. *Melius est* has a neuter adjective ('it is better'); *longius ire* has an adverb ('to go further'). Ask whether the word describes a noun or a verb.
An adverb in -e is not an ablative or a vocative. *Libenter*, *fortiter*, *prudenter* and their kind have only the one invariable form.

deeper.heading: Why the ablative?
body: Grammarians such as Allen and Greenough explain the ablative of comparison as an ablative of separation: 'stronger, starting from me'. Others see a general ablative of the standard by which one measures. The two accounts give the same forms; you do not need to decide between them to read.

deeper.heading: Comparison in late Latin
body: In later spoken Latin, comparison with a separate word, *magis* ('more'), gradually took the place of the endings, and in the Romance languages it replaced them almost entirely (as in French and Italian). The endings remain strong in the Vulgate, however, and you will meet them on every page.

quoted.english: I indeed baptize you in the water unto penance, but he that shall come after me, is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear; he shall baptize you in the Holy Ghost and fire.

examples.analysis: *fortior* is the comparative of *fortis*, nominative singular: 'stronger'. Its 'than' is the ablative of comparison, *me*: 'stronger than I', with no *quam*. (The analyser is unsure of *me* and does not mark it, but the sense is plain.)

examples.analysis: *melior* is the comparative of *bonus*: 'better'. It agrees with *acquisitio*, the subject. *negotiatione* is the ablative of comparison, 'than trading': no *quam* is used. A comparative built on a different stem from its positive is typical of the commonest adjectives.

quoted.english: A good name is better than precious ointments: and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.

examples.analysis: *Melius* is the neuter comparative of *bonus*, used as a predicate: 'it is better'. The two things compared, *nomen bonum* and *unguenta pretiosa*, are joined by *quam*, 'than', and stand in the same case, the nominative or accusative. The neuter singular is the usual way to say that something is better.

examples.analysis: *prudenter* is the adverb of *prudens*, 'wisely': the third-declension adjective takes -ter, and the form never changes. *prudentiores* is the comparative adjective, plural, agreeing with *filii*: 'wiser'. The 'than' is *filiis lucis*, the ablative of comparison, 'than the sons of light'.
